title: Variance in observations of respiratory symptoms shapes first-hand experiences
summary:
We learn not only through our own experiences, but also by observing other people (Bajcar et al., 2022; Golkar & Olsson, 2016; Haaker et al., 2017). However, such observations are less reliable than our own experiences, since we can only infer what the observed person is experiencing, but cannot feel it ourselves. This transfer from observed to personal experience becomes particularly intriguing when it involves an internal bodily sensation—a so-called interoceptive symptom—that is difficult to assess from the outside, such as breathing difficulties (Benke et al., 2021; Krause et al., 2018).
Previous studies suggest that the body’s own (endogenous) opioid system in the brain plays a central role in how we learn to recognize threats. Previous studies have already shown that blocking opioid receptors enhances learning from firsthand aversive outcomes (Eippert et al., 2008), as well as observational learning from others’ unpleasant experiences (Haaker et al., 2017).
In this study, we investigate the effect of opioid receptor blockade with the drug naltrexone on the observational learning of breathing difficulties in another person, as well as on the subsequent personal experience of artificially induced, mild shortness of breath.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-    Healthy participants
-    Right-handed
-    Fluent in German
-    Average alcohol consumption of less than 15 units per week (1 unit = 1 glass of wine, beer, or similar, and 1 cl of stronger alcoholic beverages)
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Existing or previous illnesses in the following areas:
•	Neurological or psychiatric disorders (including anxiety disorders, depression, schizophrenia, dependence on alcohol, drugs, or medication; occasional headaches excepted)
•	Cardiovascular system (including hypertension)
•	Blood/hematological disorders
•	Respiratory tract/lungs (including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, acute or chronic breathing difficulties or respiratory diseases)
•	Liver
•	Kidneys
•	Thyroid
•	Eye disorders (including glaucoma, color blindness, myopia greater than −5 diopters)
•	Skin disorders
•	Gastrointestinal tract disorders
•	Metabolic disorders
2.	Cancer (current or history of)
3.	Known allergy or intolerance to naltrexone
4.	Current medication use, or medication use within the two months prior to study participation (contraceptives excepted). Over-the-counter medications are permitted provided the last intake occurred at least one week before study participation
5.	Other serious health impairments or a pronounced current psychological or physical burden
6.	Non-removable metal objects in or on the body
7.	Possible pregnancy
8.	Current use of illegal substances
